newsitem.title: FRANCE: French MPs challenge Spanish Brigade pensions.
newsitem.headline: French MPs challenge Spanish Brigade pensions.

text.p: Some 60 conservative French parliamentarians on Friday challenged a new law granting war veteran status and pensions to an estimated 200 French survivors of the Spanish Civil War International Brigades.

The MPs asked the Constitutional Council to annul the law. They argued that the status of war veteran could be granted only to French soldiers who took part in operations ordered by the French government.
They also argued that the law, passed two weeks ago, had been tacked onto the 1997 budget bill as an irrelevant amendment.

A bill to recognise the fighting record of French citizens who fought on the side of the Republicans against the insurgent troops of General Francisco Franco had been in and out of parliament for years.

It was given a final push by President Jacques Chirac who wanted it to follow last November's national tribute to writer and long-time culture minister Andre Malraux, who led an international air squadron in the Spanish Civil War.

The veterans, who were granted Spanish citizenship last month, on the 60th anniversary of the Brigades' creation, have long campaigned for official recognition from France, arguing that they pioneered the fight against fascism before the Nazis set out to conquer Europe.
Some conservatives resisted it on grounds that the Brigades, recruited mainly by Communist parties, trade unions and other leftist groups, were heavily influenced by the Soviet Union.
France officially stayed out of the Civil War but discreetly aided the Republicans against Franco, who went on to rule Spain until his death in 1975.

Around 35,000 men and women from 53 countries fought in the International Brigades, suffering 10,000 dead and earning a place in the pantheon of left-wing heroes. A third of the 9,000 French volunteers were killed in Spain and half the survivors died in World War Two.
